title: Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. (Oct 2019 TCC) Decision
subject: Routine Engineering and Trial and Error Without Contemporaneous Records
summary: Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 246, is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision affecting Canadian manufacturers claiming investment tax credits under the Income Tax Act. The Court denied the fabricator's claims because its acrylic memorial niche work was routine engineering and trial and error, lacking contemporaneous documentation; the Federal Court of Appeal affirmed.
metaDescription: Explore the October 2019 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED ruling for Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. on Canadian R&D tax credit claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
1.1 Procedural Posture and Overview of the Dispute

On October 30, 2019, Justice John R. Owen of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) delivered the judgment in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 246 (Docket: 2016-4880(IT)G), following a trial heard in Toronto, Ontario, on October 8, 2019. The decision dismissed the taxpayer's appeals regarding reassessments issued by the Minister of National Revenue (administered by the Canada Revenue Agency, or CRA) for the 2009 and 2010 taxation years. Those reassessments disallowed the taxpayer's claims for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) current expenditures, Prescribed Proxy Amounts (PPA), qualified SR&ED expenditures, and the resulting Investment Tax Credits (ITCs).

The Tax Court's decision was subsequently appealed by the taxpayer to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (Docket: A-442-19), where a unanimous panel (Webb J.A., concurred in by Near and Boivin JJ.A.) dismissed the appeal on May 10, 2021, following an online video conference hearing held on April 27, 2021. In the appellate proceeding, the taxpayer was represented by John D. Buote of BRS Tax Lawyers LLP, while the Crown was represented by Devon E. Peavoy under Deputy Attorney General Nathalie G. Drouin. Together, the Tax Court ruling and its appellate affirmation represent a cornerstone of modern Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, definitively cementing the principle that custom engineering, material substitution, and shop-floor trial-and-error cannot qualify as SR&ED in the absence of objective technological uncertainty, rigorous adherence to the scientific method, and contemporaneous empirical documentation.
1.2 Taxpayer Profile and Technical Genesis of the Claim

Established in 1973 by its President and General Manager, Michael Bobee, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. ("Kam-Press" or the "Appellant") has carried on the business of custom manufacturing since its inception, working primarily with metal but occasionally working with other materials as the need arises. A core commercial product line of the Appellant consisted of custom-fabricated memorial niches (columbarium structures) designed to house and display funeral urns, which the Appellant had historically manufactured using standard metal framing with glass fronts.

Prior to the taxation years in issue, a commercial distributor of the Appellant's custom-manufactured products approached Kam-Press regarding the custom manufacture of a large-scale memorial niche complex for a church in Alberta. The church's architect had specified an intricate architectural geometry combining curved (arced) and straight structural sections designed to create the visual illusion that the funeral urns were "floating in space". Achieving this aesthetic specification required the memorial niche to be as transparent as possible, with lighting that supported the desired effect.

The project was overseen by Chad Bobee, the Appellant's Sales and Engineering Manager and a 30-year veteran of the company (and son of Michael Bobee), supported by long-time shop-floor personnel skilled in welding, computer numerical control (CNC) bending and cutting, costing, and three-dimensional computer-aided design (3D CAD) modeling. While the Appellant's Notice of Appeal originally encompassed multiple projects, counsel for the Appellant discontinued the appeal with respect to all projects at the commencement of the hearing except for a single overarching initiative: the Large Volume Acrylic Memorial Niche Complex Development project (the "Project"). Although the Minister's Reply to the Notice of Appeal disaggregated this work into four distinct sub-projects—namely (1) Large Volume Acrylic Memorial Niche Complex Development, (2) Memorial Niche Corner Cover Development, (3) Acrylic Memorial Niche Assembly Process Development, and (4) Memorial Niche LED Lighting Development—the Appellant clarified at trial that all four elements constituted integral components of the single overarching Project.

1.3 Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

The eligibility of expenditures for SR&ED tax incentives under the Canadian Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") operates through a two-tier statutory mechanism that has remained the structural foundation of federal R&D incentives since 1985. First, subsection 37(1) of the ITA permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current expenditures on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and to accumulate such expenditures in an indefinite carry-forward pool. Second, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, operating in conjunction with section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations"), entitle a qualifying corporation to earn Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) calculated as a percentage of its "qualified expenditure" pool, which includes the elected Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) representing notional overhead in lieu of itemized indirect expenses.

The threshold gateway to both subsection 37(1) deductions and subsection 127(5) ITCs is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" housed in subsection 248(1) of the ITA (which was transferred from Regulation 2900(1) to the ITA following earlier jurisprudence without material alteration). For industrial and manufacturing claimants, subsection 248(1) mandates that eligible work must constitute a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" falling within one of three primary categories: paragraph 248(1)(a) covering basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph 248(1)(b) covering applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; or paragraph 248(1)(c) covering experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Furthermore, paragraph 248(1)(d) incorporates "support work" undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada. Conversely, the statutory definition contains express exclusions in paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k); most notably for custom manufacturers, paragraph 248(1)(i) explicitly excludes any work with respect to the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process.

To operationalize the statutory text of subsection 248(1), Canadian courts apply the canonical five-criterion legal test formulated by Judge Donald Bowman (as he then was) at paragraph 16 of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC). As Justice Owen noted in footnote 1 to paragraph 23 of Kam-Press (citing RIS-Christie and C.W. Agencies), and as Justice Webb later reiterated on appeal (citing RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel and R&D Pro-Innovation), the Northwest Hydraulic framework has been repeatedly affirmed as the binding judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, (1998) 99 DTC 5087, C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355, R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada, 2016 FCA 152, and subsequently in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72. Under this five-part judicial test, the court evaluates: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept as the work progressed.
1.4 The Court's Final Holding and Appellate Affirmation

Justice Owen held that Kam-Press failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that the work undertaken on the Project constituted SR&ED within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Specifically, the Tax Court found that the technical challenges encountered in fabricating the acrylic memorial niche were routine engineering problems arising from the Appellant's internal lack of familiarity with acrylic polymers, that the Appellant's methodology was purely one of unsystematic "trial and error" rather than the scientific method, and that there was a complete absence of contemporaneous documentation save for retrospective summaries drafted by an external SR&ED consultant. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed with costs awarded to the Respondent in accordance with the Tariff.

When Kam-Press appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal (2021 FCA 88), its counsel conceded in paragraph 5 of its memorandum of fact and law that if Northwest Hydraulic was good law, Justice Owen's factual finding in paragraph 29—that the Appellant had not demonstrated that the procedures adopted accorded with established and objective principles of the scientific method—was fatal to the appeal. Kam-Press attempted to argue that because the phrase "scientific method" does not appear verbatim in the statutory text of subsection 248(1), the Tax Court erred in law by applying the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion. The Federal Court of Appeal summarily rejected this textualist argument, citing the Supreme Court of Canada's landmark ruling in Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54 (at para. 10), to reaffirm that the role of the court is not merely to recite exact statutory words, but to interpret provisions of the ITA and Regulations based on a textual, contextual, and purposive analysis. Finding that Kam-Press failed to address or distinguish the binding line of Federal Court of Appeal jurisprudence endorsing Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Webb dismissed the appeal with costs fixed in the amount of $1,670.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A granular examination of Justice Owen's Reasons for Judgment reveals five interlocking legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies that dismantled Kam-Press's claim. Each failure offers critical lessons for Canadian tax practitioners and engineering leaders structuring SR&ED claims.
2.1 Conflation of Subjective Enterprise Inexperience with Objective Technological Uncertainty (Criterion 1)

The foundational pillar of any experimental development claim under paragraph 248(1)(c) is the existence of a "technological risk or uncertainty". Relying on Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Owen emphasized that technological uncertainty must be an uncertainty that cannot be resolved through "routine engineering or standard procedures," where routine engineering encompasses "those techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field". Crucially, Justice Owen highlighted the legal distinction between subjective uncertainty—merely having doubt concerning how a technical problem will be solved—and objective technological uncertainty. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using standard engineering procedures accessible in the broader industry, no technological uncertainty exists, regardless of how novel or challenging the task appears to the specific taxpayer's personnel.

In Kam-Press, the taxpayer cataloged eight distinct technical challenges encountered while transitioning its memorial niche construction from traditional metal-and-glass to transparent acrylic. First, regarding base material selection, the Appellant evaluated metal-and-glass (deemed too difficult and costly to manufacture in an arced floating geometry) and tempered glass (deemed too heavy, expensive, prone to breakage in transit, and difficult to assemble without compromising structural integrity) before selecting a commercial high-grade, high-strength extruded acrylic sourced from a third-party manufacturer. Second, to achieve tight geometric tolerances so the vertical columns would align properly along a curved arc, the Appellant developed the layout using standard 3D CAD software and tested alignment via physical floor mock-ups. Third, to construct a structural base matching the column arc, the Appellant used 3D CAD software to design the base and secured the columns using custom mounts attached to the baseplates. Fourth, to construct an aluminum front beam system using interconnecting extruded and anodized aluminum beams housing LED lighting, the Appellant resolved hole-spacing issues, straight cuts for horizontal top beams, and cover plates through iterative trial modifications. Fifth, when mechanical sanding failed to dull the acrylic surface evenly to eliminate unwanted light reflectivity, the Appellant abandoned surface treatment and purchased pre-finished panels from a supplier. Sixth, to hold the acrylic pieces rigidly during gluing without flexing or shifting, the Appellant considered and rejected a two-jig system and then designed and constructed a single versatile, robust assembly jig for all columns. Seventh, when laser cutting the acrylic shapes yielded uneven edges, the Appellant switched to standard machine cutting, and when gluing the acrylic shapes failed to preserve structural integrity and optical transparency even after routing mating grooves, the Appellant outsourced the column assembly to an external acrylic manufacturing company. Eighth, when the initial LED lighting setup generated excessive heat, uneven diffusion, and visible lighting spots that could not be cured by modifying valances, lowering voltage, sandblasting tubes, or adding diffusers, the Appellant identified a different LED lighting system that eliminated the power consumption and heat issues, and designed and constructed an extruded channel-style mounting system with a diffuser cover placed in front of the LEDs.

Justice Owen did not analyze each workstream separately; he concluded that the resolution of the issues that were resolved involved the application of standard procedures or routine engineering, such as variations in the design of components, in the approaches to the assembly of components and in the materials used to construct components, and that the Appellant did not resolve or attempt to resolve any technological uncertainty. In his view, they were routine technical issues associated with the design and construction of an existing product using different materials.
2.2 The Subcontracting Evidentiary Trap and Self-Impeachment of Technological Uncertainty

Perhaps the most devastating evidentiary finding in Kam-Press arose from how the Appellant resolved its seventh technical challenge: the cutting, routing, and adhesive bonding of the transparent acrylic columns. After Kam-Press's shop-floor machinists and welders failed to glue the routed acrylic components together without compromising optical transparency or structural integrity, Kam-Press subcontracted the column assembly to an external commercial company specializing in acrylic item manufacturing.

Rather than bolstering the Appellant's narrative that acrylic bonding presented a formidable technological barrier, this outsourcing decision served as fatal self-impeachment. Justice Owen held that, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, he could only infer that the acrylic item manufacturing company had the experience and expertise to perform the required assembly. In his view, this suggested that the difficulties experienced by Kam-Press resulted from the Appellant's own internal lack of experience and expertise in polymer fabrication as a traditional metalworking shop, and not from any technological uncertainty associated with the design and construction of the memorial niches. In Canadian SR&ED litigation, when a third-party vendor can resolve the taxpayer's technical bottleneck using established commercial trade practices, the court may, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, infer that the difficulty reflects the taxpayer's own lack of experience and expertise rather than technological uncertainty, undermining the threshold requirement of Criterion 1.
2.3 Ad Hoc Trial-and-Error Versus the Total Discipline of the Scientific Method (Criteria 2 & 3)

Under the second and third Northwest Hydraulic criteria, a claimant must demonstrate that it formulated specific hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the technological uncertainty and tested those hypotheses through procedures that accord with the "total discipline of the scientific method". Citing Judge Bowman's framework, Justice Owen noted that this requires a structured five-stage investigative architecture comprising the proper observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear technological objective, the identification and precise articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of an explicit hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate that uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses through trained observation, quantitative measurement, experiment, and iterative modification of hypotheses.

In paragraph 29 of the decision, Justice Owen held squarely that Kam-Press's methodology was purely one of "trial and error". When confronted with LED hotspots or acrylic glare, the Appellant's personnel simply tried unsystematic shop-floor tweaks—sanding a panel, dropping voltage, sandblasting a tube, or routing a groove—to see what worked. Justice Owen concluded that the Appellant had not demonstrated that the procedures adopted for the Project accorded with established and objective principles of scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses. While Northwest Hydraulic recognizes that intuitive creativity and even genius may play a crucial role in uncovering and resolving new uncertainties as research progresses, Canadian jurisprudence mandates that such intuition must operate within the total discipline of the scientific method, where routine activity is distinguished from SR&ED by the adoption of the entire scientific method with a view to removing a technological uncertainty through the formulation and testing of innovative and untested hypotheses.
2.4 Absence of Technological Advancement Versus Commercial Production (Criterion 4 & Paragraph 248(1)(i))

Under the fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion and the core text of paragraph 248(1)(c), experimental development must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving a "technological advancement"—defined as an advancement in general technological understanding available to persons knowledgeable in the field. Achieving a complex commercial or architectural result by combining known materials or swapping vendor components does not constitute a technological advancement unless non-trivial combinations of established technologies and principles for their integration carry a major element of technological uncertainty, referred to in Canadian jurisprudence and CRA policy as a "system uncertainty".

In Kam-Press, whenever a shop-floor trial failed, the Appellant moved to an alternative solution: purchasing pre-finished panels to address reflectivity, identifying a different LED lighting system and designing and constructing an extruded channel-style mounting system with a diffuser cover to address the lighting issues, and subcontracting the assembly of the columns to an acrylic item manufacturing company. The goal of the Project was to develop a memorial niche that satisfied the Alberta church architect's design and aesthetic requirements; however, Justice Owen did not decide the appeals on the basis of the commercial production exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i) or make a separate finding under the fourth criterion, holding instead that the work involved standard procedures or routine engineering and that the Appellant did not resolve or attempt to resolve any technological uncertainty.
2.5 Total Absence of Contemporaneous Documentation and the Failure of Post-Facto Consultant Summaries (Criterion 5)

The fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion states that although the ITA and the Regulations do not say so explicitly, "it seems self-evident that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results be kept, and that it be kept as the work progresses". In Kam-Press, Justice Owen found a "complete absence of documentation save for the after-the-fact summaries prepared by the Appellant's SR&ED consultant".

At trial, the Appellant called three witnesses: company officers Michael Bobee and Chad Bobee, and Michael Witen, an independent SR&ED consultant retained by Kam-Press prior to and during the 2009 and 2010 taxation years. Mr. Witen had prepared a written technical narrative (entered into evidence as Exhibit A-7) describing the work undertaken by the Appellant, which Chad Bobee adopted in his testimony as an accurate description of that work. The summary in Exhibit A-7 was based on interviews with the Appellant's employees, and Justice Owen described the consultant's summaries as after-the-fact.

Justice Owen did not treat Exhibit A-7 as evidence of systematic investigation; instead, he found that his conclusion that the Appellant's approach was one of trial and error was reflected in the complete absence of documentation save for the after-the-fact summaries prepared by the consultant. Furthermore, citing RIS-Christie, Justice Owen noted that while expert testimony is not strictly required in SR&ED appeals because determining whether activities satisfy subsection 248(1) is a question of law or mixed law and fact reserved for the Tax Court judge, neither party presented an expert witness, and Justice Owen did not require the technical assistance of an expert witness to conclude that the Appellant's activities in furtherance of the Project were not SR&ED. Subsequent appellate jurisprudence, notably National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, has reinforced this exact evidentiary rule, confirming that vague or reconstructed records that fail to reflect a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result are fatal to an SR&ED appeal, and that expert reports opining on the ultimate legal question of SR&ED eligibility are inadmissible.

cells: Statutory Mandate: Experimental Development & Exclusions (ITA s. 248(1)(c), (d), and (i))

Treated custom architectural fabrication and shop-floor product design for a single church order as eligible experimental development and support work. The Tax Court did not decide the case on the commercial production exclusion or on any failure to segregate commercial order fulfillment from genuine R&ED.

Work must constitute a "systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis" to achieve technological advancement. Custom engineering for commercial production is expressly excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i), and paragraph 248(1)(d) support work is only eligible if directly supporting valid core SR&ED.
Criterion 1: Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1)

Conflated internal uncertainty regarding how to fabricate a curved, transparent memorial niche using unfamiliar material (extruded acrylic) with objective technological uncertainty. Solved geometric issues via standard 3D CAD and floor mock-ups.

Subjective doubt as to how a problem will be solved does not constitute technological uncertainty if the resolution is reasonably predictable using routine engineering or standard procedures generally accessible to competent professionals in the relevant field.
Distinction Between Enterprise Skill Deficit & Industry Knowledge Gap (Subcontracting Evidentiary Inference)

Outsourced the acrylic column gluing/assembly to a commercial acrylic item manufacturer after in-house routing and gluing trials failed. Replaced failed sanding trials with pre-finished panels and, after failed LED trials, identified a different LED lighting system with an Appellant-designed extruded channel-style mounting system and diffuser cover.

In the absence of evidence to the contrary, the fact that a third-party specialist had the experience and expertise to perform the work supports the inference that the difficulties resulted from the taxpayer's lack of experience and expertise, not from technological uncertainty.
Criterion 2: Formulation of Specific Hypotheses (Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2)
Engaged in reactive problem-solving without articulating testable causal propositions linking independent material/process variables to dependent performance failures.

Taxpayer must demonstrate a 5-stage process: (1) observation of the problem, (2) clear objective, (3) articulation of technological uncertainty, (4) formulation of specific hypotheses aimed at reducing/eliminating the uncertainty, and (5) methodical testing.
Criterion 3: Accordance with the Scientific Method (Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3)

Relied on ad hoc, unsystematic shop-floor "trial and error" (e.g., sanding panels, lowering LED voltage, sandblasting tubes, switching from laser-cut to machine-cut acrylic) without controlled experimentation or quantitative measurement. Argued on appeal that "scientific method" is not in the text of s. 248(1).

Procedures must operate within the "total discipline of the scientific method," characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, experiment, and hypothesis modification. Confirmed by 2021 FCA 88 (via Canada Trustco) as a mandatory legal requirement of s. 248(1).
Criterion 4: Technological Advancement (Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4)

Addressed the issues of the Project through third-party acrylic, pre-finished panels, 3D CAD-designed custom mounts, a different LED lighting system housed in an Appellant-designed extruded channel-style mounting system, and subcontracted column assembly; the Tax Court found this involved standard procedures or routine engineering and made no separate finding under Criterion 4.

Must seek and achieve an advancement in general technological understanding available to persons knowledgeable in the field, rather than merely achieving a new product aesthetic or solving a project-specific fabrication hurdle via standard trade practices.
Criterion 5: Contemporaneous Record-Keeping (Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5)

Maintained a complete absence of contemporaneous records generated during the 2009 and 2010 taxation years. Relied entirely on Exhibit A-7, an after-the-fact narrative summary drafted by an external SR&ED consultant based on retrospective employee interviews.

A detailed record of hypotheses, tests, measurements, and results must be kept as the work progresses. Retrospective summaries compiled by SR&ED consultants from post-project interviews carry negligible probative weight to establish systematic investigation.
Judicial Evaluation & Role of Witness / Expert Testimony (RIS-Christie Evidentiary Standard)
Relied on oral testimony of company executives (Michael and Chad Bobee) and the external SR&ED consultant (Michael Witen) to characterize shop-floor modifications as experimental development.

Determining whether activities constitute SR&ED under s. 248(1) is either a question of law or a question of mixed law and fact to be determined by the Tax Court. Expert evidence is not necessarily required; neither party called an expert, and Justice Owen did not need one to conclude that the activities were not SR&ED.

4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian industrial taxpayers and their legal and technical advisors can proactively inoculate R&D projects against the exact evidentiary and structural failures that defeated Kam-Press, the following two applied case studies present hypothetical scenarios modelled on the types of engineering challenges encountered in Kam-Press—structural polymer-to-metal hybrid fabrication and confined opto-thermal solid-state lighting integration. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial blueprint across project governance, technical documentation, contractual structuring, and experimentation tracking to satisfy subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the Northwest Hydraulic test.
4.1 Case Study 1: Structural Polymer-to-Alloy Bonding and Optical Clarity Preservation in Custom Architectural Enclosures
4.1.1 Industry Scenario & Alignment with Kam-Press Pitfalls

Vanguard Architectural Metals Inc. ("Vanguard") is an Ontario-based Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) specializing in precision CNC sheet-metal and structural steel fabrication. Vanguard is contracted by an architectural distributor to engineer a self-supporting, curved transparent structural enclosure system made of thick-gauge cast polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA / acrylic) mated to an anodized 6061-T6 aluminum load-bearing base. The architectural specification requires invisible structural joints capable of bearing a continuous vertical static load of 2.5 kN while maintaining ≥ 92% optical light transmittance across the bonded seam without mechanical fasteners.

If Vanguard approaches this project in the manner of Kam-Press—having its metal fabricators test laser versus machine cutting, routing grooves, trying commercial acrylic cements by trial and error, and ultimately subcontracting the acrylic bonding to a local plastics shop while having an external consultant write a summary at year-end—the claim will be exposed to disallowance under the reasoning of the Kam-Press precedent. To prevail at audit and before the Tax Court of Canada, Vanguard must execute a four-step remedial protocol.
4.1.2 Step 1: Project Governance & Baseline Due Diligence (Establishing Objective Technological Uncertainty)

Before commencing any shop-floor fabrication or cutting trials, Vanguard must establish through objective evidence that the inability to bond curved, thick-gauge PMMA under high structural shear stress without optical crazing is an objective limitation in polymer-to-metal materials science, rather than Vanguard's internal lack of familiarity with plastics. Vanguard's lead mechanical engineer must compile a dated Pre-Project Technological Baseline Dossier prior to initiating experimental design. This dossier must document technical consultations with PMMA resin manufacturers and industrial adhesive chemists, establishing that standard solvent welding (such as dichloromethane capillary cements) induces stress-crazing and micro-fissuring when applied to CNC-machined curved edges due to residual subsurface tooling stresses, and that standard two-part structural methacrylates create a refractive index mismatch (Δn ≈ 0.02) alongside exothermic polymerization shrinkage that destroys optical transparency across thick sections exceeding 25 mm.

Based on this baseline benchmarking, Vanguard's engineering governance committee formally defines the objective technological uncertainty in strict physical parameters: standard polymer engineering and commercial adhesive chemistries cannot simultaneously achieve a lap-shear bond strength ≥ 12 MPa and optical transmittance ≥ 92% across a 25 mm curved PMMA-to-PMMA and PMMA-to-6061-T6 interface because the thermal annealing cycle required to relieve CNC machining stresses (80 °C for 4 hours) warps the tight-tolerance arc radius (deviation beyond ±0.5 mm), whereas un-annealed bonding triggers immediate solvent-induced stress cracking. Simultaneously, to comply with the commercial production exclusion under paragraph 248(1)(i) of the ITA, project governance must formally bifurcate the enterprise resource planning (ERP) job router into two distinct accounting cost centers. Cost Center 100 (Commercial Order Fulfillment) captures all routine 3D CAD drafting of the overall architectural geometry, standard CNC cutting of aluminum baseplates, and final commercial assembly, while Cost Center 900 (SR&ED Experimental Development) is strictly restricted to investigating the coupled thermo-mechanical annealing, edge-surface energy modification, and refractive-index-matched photopolymerization process.
4.1.3 Step 2: Experimentation Tracking & Scientific Method Execution (Criteria 2, 3, and 4)

To overcome Justice Owen's finding of unsystematic "trial and error" in paragraph 29 of Kam-Press, Vanguard must implement a structured Design of Experiments (DoE) governed by the five-stage Northwest Hydraulic discipline. Rather than informally trying laser cutting versus machine cutting and routing grooves on full components, Vanguard formulates explicit, testable causal hypotheses prior to machining test coupons. Under Hypothesis H1 (Subsurface Residual Stress Attenuation), Vanguard postulates that if high-speed single-flute diamond-polished CNC end-milling is paired with localized cryogenic CO₂ vortex cooling at a feed-per-tooth of 0.08 mm and a spindle speed of 18,000 rpm, subsurface shear-zone thermal plastic deformation will remain below the critical crazing threshold of 7 MPa residual tensile stress, eliminating the need for bulk oven annealing that distorts the arc radius. Under Hypothesis H2 (Refractive-Index-Matched Silane Coupling), Vanguard postulates that formulating a custom UV-curable urethane-methacrylate oligomer blend modified with 2 wt% γ-methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane and tuned via aromatic monomer ratio to a refractive index of n = 1.491 will enable zero-visibility optical bonding across micro-routed interlocking dovetail joints while accommodating the ≈ 47 × 10⁻⁶/K coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch between PMMA and 6061-T6 aluminum without cohesive delamination.

Each experimental iteration is executed on standardized coupon specimens (25 mm × 25 mm × 100 mm curved test coupons) rather than commercial production units. Every test run systematically varies a single independent parameter (such as feed rate, coolant temperature, oligomer monomer ratio, or UV irradiance wavelength) and measures dependent outputs using calibrated laboratory instruments. Specifically, residual internal stress is measured in MPa via digital photoelastic polarimetry; surface roughness (Ra and Rz in µm) is measured via contact profilometry; bond tensile and lap-shear failure load are measured in kN via an Instron universal testing machine; and optical haze and spectral transmittance (T at 550 nm) are measured via an optical spectrophotometer. When Test Series 1.1 through 1.4 demonstrate that cryogenic cooling reduces residual stress to 4.2 MPa but causes atmospheric micro-condensation that hydrolyzes the silane coupling agent and reduces shear strength to 6.8 MPa, the engineering team formally rejects H1 as initially stated, models the moisture-hydrolysis mechanism, and formulates Modified Hypothesis H1.1 incorporating a dry-nitrogen purge shroud and low-pressure plasma surface activation. This documented progression establishes an irrefutable logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result, satisfying both Northwest Hydraulic and the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives (the "SR&ED Eligibility Guidelines").

4.1.4 Step 3: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture (Criterion 5)

To prevent the evidentiary collapse suffered by Kam-Press through its reliance on Michael Witen's post-facto Exhibit A-7 summary, Vanguard must institutionalize a real-time Contemporaneous SR&ED Evidence Repository. Every hypothesis, DoE matrix, polarimetry stress map, Instron stress-strain curve CSV export, and analytical conclusion must be logged directly by the supervising engineering personnel into a version-controlled Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) or Electronic Lab Notebook (ELN) system on the exact day the test occurs, generating immutable cryptographic timestamps. Furthermore, failed acrylic test coupons exhibiting stress crazing or cohesive shear failure are laser-engraved with their DoE Run ID, photographed under polarized light, and retained in a dedicated physical SR&ED audit bin as tangible physical evidence for inspection by the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA). Simultaneously, shop-floor technicians and engineers record their hours daily against specific SR&ED Experiment IDs—cleanly segregating paragraph 248(1)(c) experimentation and eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) testing and CAD support work from excluded commercial fabrication—while restricting external SR&ED tax advisors to formatting pre-existing contemporaneous records into Form T661 narratives.
4.1.5 Step 4: Contractual & Subcontractor Structuring (Overcoming the Outsourcing & Funded Research Traps)

In Kam-Press, outsourcing the acrylic gluing to an external acrylic manufacturer undermined Criterion 1 because, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, Justice Owen inferred that the acrylic item manufacturing company had the experience and expertise to perform the assembly, suggesting that the issues resulted from Kam-Press lacking experience and expertise in working with acrylic. Furthermore, poorly structured customer contracts with distributors can trigger "contract payment" reductions under subsection 127(18) of the ITA. If Vanguard lacks an in-house UV-curing chamber or specialized polymer chemical mixer and must engage a third-party plastics specialist ("PolyTech Ltd."), Vanguard must never issue a turn-key purchase order asking PolyTech to solve and assemble the acrylic columns. Instead, to ensure the work qualifies as SR&ED carried on "on behalf of" Vanguard under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), Vanguard must execute a formal SR&ED Subcontracting Statement of Work (SOW). This SOW must incorporate a written technical certification signed by PolyTech's chief engineer confirming that the required bond strength (≥ 12 MPa) and optical transmittance (≥ 92%) on CNC-machined curved 25 mm PMMA cannot be achieved using PolyTech's standard commercial procedures. The contract must further stipulate that PolyTech is engaged solely to perform specific curing tasks strictly in accordance with Vanguard's proprietary DoE parameter matrices and under Vanguard's direct technical supervision, that Vanguard bears 100% of the financial risk of failed test runs on a time-and-materials basis, and that Vanguard retains exclusive ownership of all resulting Intellectual Property (IP) and process know-how.

Concurrently, in its upstream commercial contract with the architectural distributor, Vanguard must structure the agreement as a fixed-price contract for the sale of a commercial good (transferring title to physical enclosure units upon delivery) rather than a contract for engineering or R&D services. The agreement must explicitly recite that any background or foreground experimental development conducted by Vanguard is undertaken at Vanguard's sole discretion, cost, and financial risk, and that the distributor acquires only the physical product with zero rights to Vanguard's manufacturing processes or IP. This contractual separation prevents customer revenue from being characterized as a government or non-government assistance or "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, preserving 100% of Vanguard's qualified SR&ED expenditure pool.
4.2 Case Study 2: Thermal Dissipation and Optical Diffusion Engineering in Confined Solid-State LED Luminaire Assemblies
4.2.1 Industry Scenario & Alignment with Kam-Press Pitfalls

LumenArc Custom Manufacturing Ltd. ("LumenArc") is a Canadian custom architectural and display manufacturer tasked with integrating high-output solid-state light-emitting diode (LED) arrays (40 W/m) inside a hermetically sealed, narrow-profile (20 mm × 25 mm) extruded aluminum and polymer structural beam system without external heat sinks or active fan cooling. During initial prototyping, LumenArc encounters severe localized thermal buildup (LED junction temperatures (Tj) exceeding 125 °C, causing rapid phosphor degradation and chromaticity shift) alongside severe optical "hot-spotting" and specular glare across adjacent transparent display panels.

In Kam-Press, the taxpayer attempted to solve similar LED lighting issues by varying the design and materials of the valance, decreasing the voltage, sandblasting the plastic tube surrounding the LEDs, and adding a thin-gauge stainless steel diffuser, and, when none of these succeeded, identified a different LED lighting system and designed and constructed an extruded channel-style mounting system with a diffuser cover. Justice Owen found that the approach of the Appellant to the issues raised by the Project was one of trial and error involving standard procedures or routine engineering, and that the Appellant had not demonstrated adherence to the scientific method (Criteria 1 and 3). LumenArc can transform this technical challenge into a fully compliant, audit-proof SR&ED claim through a disciplined four-step remediation.
4.2.2 Step 1: Project Governance & Baseline Due Diligence (Establishing Coupled "System Uncertainty")

Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence (including Northwest Hydraulic and A&D Precision Limited v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 45) recognizes that combining standard technologies, devices, or processes is eligible if non-trivial combinations of established technologies and principles for their integration carry a major element of technological uncertainty, termed a "system uncertainty". Prior to physical prototyping, LumenArc's engineering committee must compile a baseline engineering report proving an antagonistic physical trade-off that renders standard off-the-shelf LED channels, voltage dropping, and commercial diffusers unviable. Specifically, the baseline calculations demonstrate that lowering input voltage or drive current (as Kam-Press did) reduces thermal dissipation (by approximately 30%) but drops luminous flux below the mandatory architectural threshold of 4,000 lm/m. Conversely, inserting dense optical diffuser plates or sandblasting optical surfaces (as Kam-Press did) eliminates LED hot-spots by increasing Mie optical scattering, but increases photon back-reflection and internal cavity absorption by 15–20%, trapping radiant heat inside the hermetically sealed 20 mm channel and driving the LED junction temperature (Tj) above the maximum rated limit of 125 °C. Meanwhile, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) extruded aluminum LED channels require convective air volume or external fin surface area (≥ 150 cm² per metre) that violates the structural beam interlock geometry.

Having documented why standard optoelectronic engineering fails, LumenArc formally articulates the objective technological uncertainty: whether a passive, hermetically sealed micro-extrusion (20 mm × 25 mm) can achieve continuous thermal dissipation of 40 W/m (maintaining LED junction temperature Tj ≤ 105 °C at 35 °C ambient) while simultaneously achieving a spatial luminance uniformity ratio (Lmin/Lmax) ≥ 0.85 and optical transmission efficiency ≥ 88% across a short 8 mm optical mixing distance.
4.2.3 Step 2: Experimentation Tracking & Scientific Method Execution (Criteria 2, 3, and 4)

Instead of unsystematic shop-floor modifications, LumenArc structures a multi-iteration scientific investigation combining computational physics with empirical laboratory testing. The engineering team formulates two primary multi-physics hypotheses. Under Hypothesis H1 (Anisotropic Thermal Interface & Micro-Groove Radiation Architecture), LumenArc hypothesizes that coating the internal 6063-T5 aluminum extrusion cavity with a 30 µm plasma-electrolytic oxidation (PEO) ceramic dielectric layer doped with hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and micro-machining asymmetric internal parabolic facets will reduce junction-to-case thermal resistance (Rth(j-c)) by 25% via direct metal-core PCB-to-wall conduction while redirecting back-scattered photons forward without thermal absorption. Under Hypothesis H2 (Volumetric Refractive Micro-Lenticular Polymer Co-Extrusion), LumenArc hypothesizes that replacing surface sandblasting (which Kam-Press attempted without satisfactorily solving its lighting issues, and which in this scenario causes isotropic back-scatter and heat trapping) with a custom-compounded polycarbonate diffuser doped with 0.5–1.5 wt% core-shell silicone-acrylate microspheres (2 µm diameter) and an interior Fresnel micro-lenticular pitch of 0.3–0.5 mm will achieve total internal reflection (TIR) homogenization at an 8 mm throw distance with ≤ 12% optical insertion loss.

To test these hypotheses systematically, engineers first execute finite-element thermal simulations (ANSYS Icepak) and Monte Carlo non-sequential ray-tracing simulations (Zemax OpticStudio) to predict thermal gradients and candela distributions prior to physical tooling. Subsequently, across 12 documented experimental prototypes (Prototypes E-01 through E-12), LumenArc holds PCB power density constant at 40 W/m and systematically alters PEO coating thickness, microsphere concentration, and lenticular pitch. Every test run records steady-state temperature profiles across 16 K-type thermocouples logged at 1-second intervals over 6-hour thermal soak tests, measures solder-point temperature (Ts) to calculate Tj, quantifies total luminous flux (lm) and luminous efficacy (lm/W) inside a 1.5 m integrating sphere, and maps spatial luminance uniformity (Lmin/Lmax) via a 2D imaging photometer. Even when intermediate prototypes fail due to dielectric micro-cracking at elevated temperatures, the systematic characterization of the coupled thermo-optical transfer function between microsphere Mie scattering and internal cavity thermal impedance constitutes an objective advancement in opto-thermal packaging knowledge.

4.2.4 Step 3: Contemporaneous Documentation Architecture (Criterion 5)

To satisfy Criterion 5 and avoid the fatal evidentiary gap identified by Justice Owen in Kam-Press, all thermocouple CSV logs, integrating-sphere spectral power distribution reports, and Zemax/ANSYS simulation files are automatically archived with system-generated timestamps in an immutable cloud repository. In addition, the R&D team conducts bi-weekly engineering design reviews where contemporaneously recorded minutes follow a strict four-part structure aligned with the CRA's SR&ED Eligibility Guidelines: the specific hypothesis tested since the prior review, the quantitative test parameters and empirical measurements obtained, the logical conclusions drawn from the data, and the modified hypothesis formulated for the next iteration. If LumenArc engages an external SR&ED consultant, the consultant is onboarded during the active fiscal year solely to audit the completeness of the contemporaneous engineering logs in real time, ensuring that no retrospective interview-based summaries (such as Exhibit A-7 in Kam-Press) are ever tendered as primary evidence.
4.2.5 Step 4: Contractual & Subcontractor Structuring

When LumenArc engages an external aluminum extruder or polymer compounder to produce experimental test batches (Prototypes E-01 to E-12), the vendor contracts must explicitly specify that the vendor is manufacturing custom experimental test coupons to LumenArc's proprietary CAD dies and chemical formulations, rather than supplying standard catalog items. Vendor invoices must reference the exact Experimental Run IDs (for example, "Custom Co-Extrusion Trial Run E-05 per LumenArc Spec Rev 2 - Non-Commercial Prototype") so the costs clearly qualify as materials transformed or consumed in SR&ED under subsection 37(1).

Furthermore, suppose that after several months of rigorous, documented experimentation (Runs E-01 through E-07), the commercial client refuses to wait longer and forces LumenArc to relax the architectural beam dimensions and install a standard commercial LED strip to meet a construction deadline—mirroring Kam-Press's eventual move to a different LED lighting system housed in an extruded channel-style mounting system with a diffuser cover. Because commercial or technical success is not a prerequisite for SR&ED eligibility under Canadian law (Northwest Hydraulic), LumenArc's contemporaneous documentation of Runs E-01 through E-07 preserves 100% of the SR&ED claim up to the exact date the experimental program was halted, provided LumenArc formally executes a dated Technical Project Closure Memo closing the SR&ED accounting cost center prior to purchasing and installing the commercial off-the-shelf LED system under its commercial production cost center.

5. Conclusion & Strategic Advisory Synthesis

The Tax Court of Canada's ruling in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 246), together with its unequivocal endorsement by the Federal Court of Appeal (2021 FCA 88) and subsequent reinforcement in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), removes any lingering ambiguity regarding the evidentiary and methodological thresholds governing Canada's SR&ED tax incentive program. Even following the CRA's replacement, on August 13, 2021, of its Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy with the SR&ED Eligibility Guidelines—which streamlined administrative phrasing into "Why" (whether work is conducted to advance scientific knowledge or achieve technological advancement) and "How" (whether work is conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by experiment or analysis)—the Federal Court of Appeal has expressly confirmed that administrative guidelines do not alter statutory law, and that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the mandatory legal test under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

For Canadian corporations and their legal and technical advisors, Kam-Press establishes three overarching compliance imperatives that must govern every SR&ED claim prior to filing Form T661. First, objective baseline benchmarking must precede shop-floor execution: a claimant must rigorously distinguish between an internal enterprise skill deficit (such as a traditional metal fabricator working with structural acrylic for the first time) and an objective gap in industry-wide technological knowledge. Where a third-party specialist can perform the work that the taxpayer could not, the court may infer, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the difficulties stem from the taxpayer's lack of experience and expertise rather than technological uncertainty, leaving the work to be characterized as routine engineering and disqualified ab initio. Second, ad hoc shop-floor trial and error must be replaced by quantitative hypothesis testing: reactive adjustments—no matter how numerous, costly, or commercially necessary—fail the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion unless anchored in explicit causal hypotheses, controlled variable isolation, and quantitative empirical measurement operating within the total discipline of the scientific method. Finally, contemporaneous documentation cannot be cured retroactively: the practice of relying on external SR&ED consultants to prepare after-the-fact summaries based on employee interviews (as exemplified by Exhibit A-7 in Kam-Press) did not save the claim in Kam-Press, where Justice Owen found a complete absence of documentation save for those after-the-fact summaries. Without dated, contemporaneous records of hypotheses, empirical test data, and logical conclusions generated as the work progresses, even technically ambitious industrial projects face summary disallowance at audit and certain dismissal before the Tax Court of Canada.
